analysis.one_liner: Created military tribunals for non-citizen terror suspects and stripped their right to challenge detention in court.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 253–168, mostly along party lines, but the Senate never voted on this bill — though Congress enacted the same plan through a companion Senate bill that fall.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court threw out the Bush administration's earlier system of military tribunals, this bill wrote a new one into law. It set up military commissions to try non-citizen 'unlawful enemy combatants' for war crimes, allowed the death penalty, and barred detainees from citing the Geneva Conventions as a source of rights in court. It also shut the courthouse door: federal courts could no longer hear habeas corpus challenges — the classic legal vehicle for asking a judge 'why am I being held?' — from any non-citizen detained abroad by the U.S. And it required the government to pay the legal bills of government personnel sued over interrogations conducted between 2001 and 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: The executive branch gains the most: a permanent, congressionally approved tribunal system for trying captured suspects, unilateral presidential authority to interpret the Geneva Conventions, retroactive legal protection and fee payments for interrogators and other personnel facing civil suits or prosecution over 2001–2005 interrogations, and the elimination of court review of detention decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The executive branch and government personnel

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the President to establish military commissions to try alien unlawful enemy combatants for law-of-war violations, with procedures codified in statute rather than left to executive order.

Includes real procedural safeguards: no compelled self-incrimination, a ban on statements obtained by torture (with a narrow exception), required military defense counsel, a presumption of innocence, and a prohibition on cruel or unusual punishments.
Prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment of any person in U.S. custody, regardless of nationality or location.

Requires the government to provide counsel and pay legal fees for U.S. personnel facing civil or criminal actions arising out of authorized interrogations conducted between September 11, 2001 and December 30, 2005.

analysis.who_pays: Non-citizens detained by the United States bear the cost: they lose the right to file habeas corpus or any other court challenge to their detention, treatment, or trial — including cases already pending — and cannot invoke the Geneva Conventions as a source of rights. Federal courts lose jurisdiction over these cases. Taxpayer money goes to legal defense of government personnel.

drawbacks.text: The bill strips courts of jurisdiction to hear habeas corpus or any other action relating to detention, treatment, or trial of aliens detained outside the United States, applying immediately to all cases pending on or after enactment — meaning a person could be held with no way to ask a judge whether the detention is lawful.

A statement obtained before December 30, 2005, in which the degree of coercion is disputed, can be admitted if the military judge finds it reliable — so testimony gathered under disputed coercion could still be used in a case carrying life imprisonment or death.

Rules of evidence are loosened relative to courts-martial: hearsay not normally admissible can be admitted, evidence seized without a warrant is not excluded, and the accused can be excluded from hearings where classified evidence is argued.

A tribunal's determination that a person is an 'unlawful enemy combatant' is dispositive for jurisdiction, and the President is authorized to issue his own interpretations of the Geneva Conventions by executive order.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does create a functioning legal system with some genuine safeguards — military defense counsel, a bar on torture-obtained statements, a ban on cruel treatment — which is more than the improvised system the Supreme Court had rejected. But the design leans heavily toward the government: the accused cannot invoke the Geneva Conventions, cannot go to any court to challenge detention, faces looser evidence rules than an American would in criminal court, and the President gets to define what the treaty means. The core trade-off the House accepted was speed and executive flexibility at the price of independent judicial review — and it took that trade in a bill closed to amendments and debated for two hours.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a 253–168 vote but the Senate never took it up; it sat in the Senate Armed Services Committee until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced September 25, 2006, and referred to three House committees, it was brought to the floor the next day under a rule that allowed two hours of debate, closed the bill to amendments, and deemed a Rules Committee amendment adopted.

On September 27, 2006, the House rejected a motion to recommit with instructions — which would have added expedited judicial review — by 228 to 195, with 189 of 201 House Democrats in favor and 223 of 230 Republicans opposed.
The House then passed the bill 253–168, with 219 of 231 Republicans in favor and only 34 of 201 Democrats; the one Independent voted no.
The Senate received the bill the same day but did not refer it to committee until November 13, 2006, and it never received a Senate vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch and government interrogators ultimately came out ahead: although this House bill itself died in the Senate, Congress passed a Senate companion with the same core provisions in mid-October 2006, and President Bush signed it into law — delivering the tribunals, the habeas strip-out, and the interrogation protections despite the House bill's fate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The executive branch and government personnel

for.name: Duncan Hunter
for.role: House Armed Services Committee Chairman and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the House as Armed Services chairman.

for.name: 219 of 231 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, providing nearly all of the votes needed to pass the bill.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Urged Congress to quickly enact legislation restoring military commissions after the Supreme Court's Hamdan decision struck down the prior system.

against.name: Ike Skelton
against.role: Ranking Democrat, House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add a section providing expedited judicial review; the motion failed 195–228.

against.name: 160 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage after their motion to recommit was voted down.

against.name: 7 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans opposed to the bill

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split sharply by party: 219 of 231 Republicans voted yes while 160 of 201 Democrats voted no (34 Democrats joined); the failed motion to recommit split almost perfectly along party lines, 189–5 among Democrats and 5–223 among Republicans.

industries.industry: The executive branch and U.S. government interrogators
industries.note: The bill gives the executive a permanent statutory tribunal system, lets the President alone interpret the Geneva Conventions, shields interrogators and other personnel by requiring the government to defend and pay for their legal costs in suits over 2001–2005 interrogations, and cuts courts out of detention review. The cost falls on detainees' access to any court.

Courts lose jurisdiction over habeas petitions and other challenges from detained aliens, including cases already pending, and their review of commission verdicts is confined to questions of law in a narrow channel. This removes judicial checks that protect anyone the government might detain.

industries.industry: Detained non-citizens and the lawyers who represent them
industries.note: Alien unlawful enemy combatants are barred from invoking the Geneva Conventions as a source of rights and from filing habeas corpus petitions, and civilian defense counsel must clear security checks and sign compliance agreements to appear. Their interest in court access runs directly against the government's interest in unreviewable detention.
